passages.source_text: οὗτοι τῷ ἐνταῦθα ἐπιδημήσαντι Ζακχαίῳ συντυχόντες καὶ τοῦ τῆς ἀληθείας δι’ αὐτοῦ μεταλαβόντες λόγου, ἐπὶ τοῖς πρώτοις νεωτερισμοῖς μεταμεληθέντες, ταχέως τοῦ Σίμωνος καταγνόντες, πάντα αὐτῷ συνειδότες, ἅμα τῷ ἐπιδημῆσαί με ἐνταῦθα μετὰ τῆς ἀναθρεψαμένης αὐτοὺς προσελθόντες μοι, ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ συσταθέντες μοι, καὶ ἔκτοτε πάντοτε σύνεισίν μοι, τῶν τῆς ἀληθείας ἀπολαύοντες μαθημάτων. ταῦτα εἰπὼν ὁ Πέτρος, μεταπεμψάμενος ἐκέλευσεν αὐτοῖς πάντα μοι τὰ κατὰ τὸν Σίμωνα ἀκριβῶς ἐκτίθεσθαι. οἱ δὲ τὸν θεὸν μαρτυράμενοι μηδὲν ψεύσασθαι, ἐξετίθεντο.

ὧν πρῶτος ὁ Ἀκύλας ἤρξατο λέγειν οὕτως Ἄκουσον, φίλτατε ἡμῖν ἀδελφέ, ὅπως ἀκριβῶς πάντα τὰ κατὰ τὸν ἄνδρα εἰδῇς, τίνος τε ὢν καὶ τίς καὶ πόθεν, τίνα τε ἐστὶν ἃ πράττει καὶ πῶς καὶ διὰ τί. Σίμων οὗτος πατρὸς μὲν ἐστὶν Ἀντωνίου, μητρὸς δὲ Ῥαχήλ, σαμαρεὺς τὸ ἔθνος, ἀπὸ Γετθῶν κώμης, τῆς πόλεως ἀπεχούσης σχοίνους ἕξ. οὗτος ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τῇ πρὸς Αἴγυπτον γεγονώς, ἑλληνικῇ παιδείᾳ πάνυ ἐξασκήσας ἑαυτὸν καὶ μαγείᾳ πολὺ δυνηθεὶς καὶ φρενωθεὶς θέλει νομίζεσθαι ἀνωτάτη τις εἶναι δύναμις καὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον κτίσαντος θεοῦ, ἐνίοτε δὲ καὶ χριστὸν ἑαυτὸν αἰνισσόμενος, ἑστῶτα προσαγορεύει. ταύτῃ δὲ τῇ προσηγορίᾳ κέχρηται, ὡς δὴ στησόμενος ἀεὶ καὶ αἰτίαν φθορᾶς, ὥστε τὸ σῶμα πεσεῖν , οὐκ ἔχων. καὶ οὔτε θεὸν τὸν κτίσαντα τὸν κόσμον ἀνώτατον εἶναι λέγει. οὐ νεκροὺς ἐγερθήσεσθαι πιστεύει. τὴν Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἀρνεῖται, τὸ Γαριζεὶν ὄρος ἀντεισφέρει. ἀντὶ τοῦ ὄντος χριστοῦ ἡμῶν ἑαυτὸν ἀναγορεύει. τὰ δὲ τοῦ νόμου ἰδίᾳ προλήψει ἀλληγορεῖ. καὶ κρίσιν ἔσεσθαι μὲν λέγει, οὐ προσδοκᾷ δέ· οὐ γὰρ ἂν ὑπὸ θεοῦ κριθήσεσθαι πεπεισμένος μέχρι αὐτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀσεβεῖν ἐτόλμα. ὅθεν ἔνιοι μὴ εἰδότες ὅτι προκαλύμματι τῇ θεοσεβείᾳ κεχρημένος ὑποσυλᾷ τὰ τῆς ἀληθείας καὶ τὴν ὁπώσποτε ὑπὸ αὐτοῦ ἐλπίδα καὶ κρίσιν λεγομένην ἔσεσθαι, ὡς πιστῶς πιστεύοντες ἀπόλλυνται.

τὸ δὲ παρεισελθεῖν αὐτὸν τὸν τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγον γέγονεν οὕτως· Ἰωάννης τις ἐγένετο ἡμεροβαπτιστής, ὃς καὶ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ κατὰ τὸν τῆς συζυγίας λόγον ἐγένετο πρόοδος· καὶ ὥσπερ τῷ κυρίῳ γεγόνασιν δώδεκα ἀπόστολοι, τῶν τοῦ ἡλίου δώδεκα μηνῶν φέροντες τὸν ἀριθμόν, ὡσαύτως καὶ αὐτῷ ἕξαρχοι ἄνδρες γεγόνασιν τριάκοντα, τὸν μηνιαῖον τῆς σελήνης ἀποπληροῦντες λόγον. ἐν ᾧ ἀριθμῷ μία τις ἦν γυνὴ λεγομένη Ἑλένη, ἵνα μηδὲ τοῦτο ἀνοικονόμητον ᾖ. ἥμισυ γὰρ ἀνδρὸς οὖσα ἡ γυνὴ ἀτελῆ τὸν τῆς τριακοντάδος τέθεικεν ἀριθμόν, ὥσπερ καὶ τῆς σελήνης, ἧς ἡ πορεία τοῦ μηνὸς οὐ τέλειον ποιεῖται τὸν δρόμον. τούτων δὲ τῶν τριάκοντα τῷ Ἰωάννῃ πρῶτος καὶ δοκιμώτατος ἦν ὁ Σίμων, ὃς καὶ τοῦ μὴ ἄρξαι αὐτὸν μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν τοῦ Ἰωάννου αἰτίαν ἔσχεν ταύτην·

ἀποδημοῦντος γὰρ αὐτοῦ εἰς Αἴγυπτον ἐπὶ τὴν τῆς μαγείας ἐπάσκησιν, τοῦ Ἰωάννου ἀναιρεθέντος, Δοσίθεός τις τῆς ἀρχῆς ὀρεγόμενος, θάνατον αὐτοῦ ψευδῆ καταγγείλας διαδέχεται τὴν αἵρεσιν. ὁ δὲ Σίμων μετ’ οὐ πολὺ ἐπελθὼν καὶ τοῦ τόπου ὡς ἰδίου μεγάλως ἀντεχόμενος, τῷ Δοσιθέῳ συντυχὼν τὸν μὲν τόπον οὐκ ἀπῄτει, εἰδὼς ὅτι ὁ φθάσας τῆς ἀρχῆς παρὰ προαίρεσιν οὐ καθαιρεῖται. διὸ μετὰ προσποιητοῦ φιλίας ἐπ’ ὀλίγον μὲν εἰς τὸν δεύτερον τοῦ Δοσιθέου τόπον δίδωσιν ἑαυτόν. ταγεὶς δὲ μετ’ οὐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας τοῖς τριάκοντα συμμαθηταῖς, ὑποδιαβάλλειν ἤρξατο τὸν Δοσίθεον, ὡς μὴ παραδιδόντα γνησίως τὰ μαθήματα. καὶ τοῦτο ποιεῖν ἔλεγεν αὐτὸν οὐχ ὡς φθονοῦντα, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἀγνοοῦντα. καὶ ποτὲ ὁ Δοσίθεος, ὑπαισθόμενος τὴν τοῦ Σίμωνος ἔντεχνον διαβολὴν λύουσαν αὐτοῦ τὴν πρὸς τοὺς πολλοὺς ὑπόνοιαν, τοῦ μὴ αὐτὸν εἶναι νομίζειν τὸν ἑστῶτα, θυμῷ ἐπὶ τὴν συνήθη παραγενόμενος διατριβὴν ῥάβδῳ παίει εὑρὼν τὸν Σίμωνα· ἡ δὲ ὥσπερ καπνοῦ τοῦ Σίμωνος διελθεῖν ἔδοξε σῶμα. ἐπὶ τούτῳ καταπλαγεὶς ὁ Δοσίθεος λέγει αὐτῷ Εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ ἑστώς, καὶ προσκυνῶ σε. τοῦ Σίμωνος εἰπόντος Ἐγώ εἰμι, ὁ Δοσίθεος ἑαυτὸν γνοὺς οὐκ ὄντα τὸν ἑστῶτα, πεσὼν προσεκύνησεν, καὶ τοῖς εἰκοσιεννέα ἑξάρχοις συγκαταβαλὼν ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ τῆς ὑπονοίας τόπον ἔστησε τὸν Σίμωνα, καὶ οὕτως μετ’ οὐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας ὁ Δοσίθεος, ἐκείνου στάντος, αὐτὸς πεσὼν ἐτελεύτησεν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.

passages.text: These men met Zacchaeus while he was staying here and, through him, shared in the word of truth. Having regretted their initial innovations, they quickly condemned Simon. Since they had shared knowledge of everything with him, as soon as I arrived here they approached me together with the woman who had raised them. They were introduced to me by Zacchaeus, and from then on they have always remained with me, benefiting from the teachings of the truth. After Peter said this, he sent for them and ordered them to set out for me precisely everything concerning Simon. They called God as witness that they would tell no lie, and began their account.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Having regretted their initial innovations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb expresses regret over their earlier innovations; the context does not require the policy term “reorient.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Since they had shared knowledge of everything with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction can denote being privy to everything together with Simon; “knowing everything about him” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: together with the woman who had raised them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle identifies a woman, and the verb denotes bringing up or rearing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: They were introduced to me by Zacchaeus
lexical_decisions.rationale: Zacchaeus is the contextually preferable antecedent of the pronoun, and the verb here denotes presenting or introducing someone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: benefiting from the teachings of the truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle can mean enjoying, partaking of, or benefiting from the instruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: They called God as witness that they would tell no lie
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction invokes God as witness to the truthfulness of the account they are about to give.

source_issues.issue: The pronoun can grammatically refer to more than one previously mentioned man. The main text chooses Zacchaeus because he had instructed them locally and could naturally introduce them to Peter; reference to Simon is contextually less likely.

passages.text: Of these, Aquila was the first and began to speak as follows: “Listen, brother dearest to us, so that you may know precisely everything concerning the man—whose son he is, who he is and where he comes from, what things he does, and how and why. This Simon’s father is Antonius and his mother Rachel. He is a Samaritan by nationality, from Geththon, a village six schoeni from the city. Having been in Alexandria in Egypt, he thoroughly trained himself in Greek learning, became very powerful in magic, and grew conceited. He wants to be regarded as some supreme power, higher even than the God who created the world. At times, while also hinting that he himself is the Messiah, he calls himself ‘the Standing One.’ He uses this designation on the ground that he will always stand and has no cause of decay that would make his body fall. Nor does he say that the God who created the world is supreme. He does not believe that the dead will be raised. He repudiates Jerusalem and advances Mount Gerizim in opposition to it. In place of our actual Messiah, he proclaims himself. He allegorizes the provisions of the Law according to his own preconception. He says that there will be a judgment, but he does not expect it; for if he were convinced that he would be judged by God, he would not have dared to act impiously even against God himself. Consequently, some people, unaware that he uses reverence for God as a veil and stealthily pilfers what belongs to the truth, perish as people faithfully believing in the hope and judgment that he says will somehow come to pass.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Listen, brother dearest to us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording explicitly preserves the group relationship expressed by ἡμῖν, presenting the addressed brother as dear to Aquila and his companions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνος τε ὢν καὶ τίς καὶ πόθεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son he is, who he is and where he comes from
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first expression concerns family origin here, as the immediately following identification of Simon’s parents indicates.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a Samaritan by nationality
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase identifies Simon’s ethnic or national affiliation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from Geththon, a village
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Geththon” directly represents the printed place name; Gitta and Gittha are possible conventional forms.

lexical_decisions.chosen: six schoeni
lexical_decisions.rationale: The schoenus was an ancient unit of variable length, so retaining it avoids an unsupported modern conversion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τῇ πρὸς Αἴγυπτον γεγονώς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Having been in Alexandria in Egypt
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the broad force of the expression without deciding whether it denotes residence, presence, or birth; “having been born in Alexandria in Egypt” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνωτάτη τις εἶναι δύναμις καὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον κτίσαντος θεοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: some supreme power, higher even than the God who created the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive associated with the superlative presents Simon’s claimed power as surpassing even the creator God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hinting that he himself is the Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes suggesting indirectly, while χριστός functions independently as a title.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he calls himself ‘the Standing One’
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect participle functions as a designation and begins the section’s repeated standing-and-falling imagery.

lexical_decisions.chosen: advances Mount Gerizim in opposition to it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb means to bring forward as a counterclaim or substitute; Jerusalem is the contextual point of opposition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: In place of our actual Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle contrasts the real or actual Messiah with Simon’s self-proclamation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δὲ τοῦ νόμου ἰδίᾳ προλήψει ἀλληγορεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: He allegorizes the provisions of the Law according to his own preconception
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes a prior assumption or preconceived notion governing his allegorical treatment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he uses reverence for God as a veil
lexical_decisions.rationale: Reverence for God is presented as a covering or façade.

lexical_decisions.chosen: perish as people faithfully believing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering represents ὡς as characterizing the capacity or stance in which they perish and renders the adverb and verb as “faithfully believing.” The alternative “perish as though believing faithfully” takes ὡς as marking a supposed or represented stance.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τῇ πρὸς Αἴγυπτον γεγονώς
source_issues.issue: The participle can describe having been or lived in Alexandria, but it can also denote having been born there. The main wording leaves that distinction open.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ τῆς ἀληθείας καὶ τὴν ὁπώσποτε ὑπὸ αὐτοῦ ἐλπίδα καὶ κρίσιν λεγομένην ἔσεσθαι, ὡς πιστῶς πιστεύοντες ἀπόλλυνται
source_issues.issue: The syntax is compressed. The main text takes the hope and judgment as the content of πιστεύοντες, but they may instead be included among the things of truth that Simon stealthily appropriates. The placement of ὁπώσποτε permits either “which he says will somehow occur” or “which he somehow says will occur.” The main text takes ὡς as characterizing the people as faithful believers; it may instead present their stance as supposed: “as though believing faithfully.”

passages.text: The way he slipped into the doctrine of reverence for God came about as follows: There was a certain John, a daily baptizer, who, according to the principle of pairing, also became the forerunner of our Lord Jesus. Just as our Lord had twelve apostles, bearing the number of the sun’s twelve months, so John too had thirty leading men, fulfilling the moon’s monthly reckoning. Within that number there was one woman named Helena, so that not even this might lie outside the ordered scheme. For the woman, being half a man, made the count of the thirty incomplete, just as the moon’s count is incomplete, since the moon’s journey does not complete its course during the month. Of these thirty, Simon was first and most highly approved by John. The reason he did not assume leadership after John’s death was this:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δὲ παρεισελθεῖν αὐτὸν τὸν τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: The way he slipped into the doctrine of reverence for God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb suggests intrusive or surreptitious entry, while λόγος here denotes a body of teaching.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a daily baptizer
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound describes one who practices daily baptism; “Hemerobaptist” would be a possible technical transliteration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: according to the principle of pairing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes a pairing or paired correspondence within the work’s conceptual scheme.

lexical_decisions.chosen: became the forerunner
lexical_decisions.rationale: The predicate noun concerns going forth or going before and identifies John’s precursor role.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν τοῦ ἡλίου δώδεκα μηνῶν φέροντες τὸν ἀριθμόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: bearing the number of the sun’s twelve months
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source explicitly correlates the twelve apostles with the twelve solar months.

lexical_decisions.chosen: had thirty leading men
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes chiefs or leading persons. The following sentences explicitly include one woman within this numbered group.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that not even this might lie outside the ordered scheme
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective describes something unarranged or outside an ordering plan.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥμισυ γὰρ ἀνδρὸς οὖσα ἡ γυνὴ
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the woman, being half a man
lexical_decisions.rationale: The author’s gendered numerical claim is translated directly without endorsement or mitigation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀτελῆ τὸν τῆς τριακοντάδος τέθεικεν ἀριθμόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: made the count of the thirty incomplete
lexical_decisions.rationale: Within the author’s calculation, Helena’s inclusion produces an incomplete total corresponding to the lunar course.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἧς ἡ πορεία τοῦ μηνὸς οὐ τέλειον ποιεῖται τὸν δρόμον
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the moon’s journey does not complete its course during the month
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τοῦ μηνός temporally, setting the period during which the moon’s journey fails to complete its course. It may instead modify τὸν δρόμον: “whose movement does not cover the month’s course in full.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρῶτος καὶ δοκιμώτατος ἦν ὁ Σίμων
lexical_decisions.chosen: Simon was first and most highly approved
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative can mean most approved, esteemed, tested, or qualified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he did not assume leadership
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb here concerns taking the leading position after John rather than merely beginning an action.

source_issues.source_quote: μία τις ἦν γυνὴ λεγομένη Ἑλένη
source_issues.issue: The source has just described the numbered group as thirty ἄνδρες but then states that one member was a woman. The following explanation deliberately develops this numerical tension, so no correction is warranted.

source_issues.source_quote: ἧς ἡ πορεία τοῦ μηνὸς οὐ τέλειον ποιεῖται τὸν δρόμον
source_issues.issue: The genitive τοῦ μηνός may be temporal, as in the main text, or may attach to τὸν δρόμον, yielding “whose movement does not cover the month’s course in full.” This is an attachment ambiguity rather than evidence of source corruption.

source_issues.source_quote: τῷ Ἰωάννῃ πρῶτος καὶ δοκιμώτατος ἦν ὁ Σίμων
source_issues.issue: The dative may present Simon as first and most approved in John’s estimation or place him first within the group associated with John. The main text combines rank within the group with John’s approval.

passages.text: For while Simon was away in Egypt to advance his training in magic, John was killed. A certain Dositheus, who coveted the leadership, falsely announced Simon’s death and succeeded to the sect. Simon returned not long afterward and, though he laid strong claim to the position as his own, when he met Dositheus he did not demand it back, knowing that the person who first secures the leadership is not deposed against his will. Therefore, under a pretense of friendship, he submitted himself for a little while to second place under Dositheus. After not many days, once he had been ranked among the thirty fellow disciples, he began secretly to disparage Dositheus, alleging that he was not transmitting the teachings authentically. He said that Dositheus did this not out of envy but out of ignorance. At one point Dositheus perceived that Simon’s artful disparagement was destroying the estimation in which the majority held him, so that he was thought not to be the Standing One. He came in anger to their customary session and, finding Simon, struck him with a staff; but the staff seemed to pass through Simon’s body as though it were smoke. Astonished at this, Dositheus said to him, “If you are the Standing One, then I worship you.” When Simon said, “I am,” Dositheus recognized that he himself was not the Standing One, fell down, and worshiped him. He lowered himself to the level of the twenty-nine chief disciples and made Simon stand in the place in their estimation that had been his own. And so, after not many days, while Simon stood, Dositheus himself fell and died.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to advance his training in magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes continued practice, training, or cultivation of an ability.

lexical_decisions.chosen: falsely announced Simon’s death
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronoun most naturally refers to the absent Simon, whose supposed death would remove his claim to succeed John.

lexical_decisions.chosen: succeeded to the sect
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes taking over in succession, while αἵρεσις here refers to the organized school or sect.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ τόπου ὡς ἰδίου μεγάλως ἀντεχόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: though he laid strong claim to the position as his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: The “place” is the leadership position, and the verb expresses holding firmly to or asserting a claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is not deposed against his will
lexical_decisions.rationale: The prepositional phrase is understood as removal contrary to the officeholder’s choice; “regardless of preference” is less likely.

lexical_decisions.chosen: under a pretense of friendship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression presents friendship as assumed or feigned.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν δεύτερον τοῦ Δοσιθέου τόπον δίδωσιν ἑαυτόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: he submitted himself for a little while to second place under Dositheus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase places Simon in a subordinate, second-ranking position relative to Dositheus.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταγεὶς δὲ μετ’ οὐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας τοῖς τριάκοντα συμμαθηταῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: After not many days, once he had been ranked among the thirty fellow disciples
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative is taken as the group to which Simon was assigned, though appointment in relation to or over them is also grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he began secretly to disparage Dositheus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound denotes covert or insinuating slander.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς μὴ παραδιδόντα γνησίως τὰ μαθήματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: alleging that he was not transmitting the teachings authentically
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb can mean genuinely, faithfully, or authentically.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the estimation in which the majority held him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun is taken as the opinion or supposition about Dositheus among the wider group; “suspicion” is possible lexically but less suitable here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ δὲ ὥσπερ καπνοῦ τοῦ Σίμωνος διελθεῖν ἔδοξε σῶμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: but the staff seemed to pass through Simon’s body as though it were smoke
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun refers back to the staff, while the smoke comparison characterizes Simon’s apparently insubstantial body.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ ἑστώς, καὶ προσκυνῶ σε
lexical_decisions.chosen: If you are the Standing One, then I worship you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conjunction is taken with apodotic force; “I too worship you” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He lowered himself to the level of the twenty-nine chief disciples
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle depicts Dositheus lowering himself into the rank associated with the twenty-nine leaders.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ τῆς ὑπονοίας τόπον ἔστησε τὸν Σίμωνα
lexical_decisions.chosen: made Simon stand in the place in their estimation that had been his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: Rendering ἔστησε as “made stand” preserves the sustained standing-and-falling imagery. The unusual genitive phrase is taken as Dositheus’s former place in the group’s estimation, though it may instead concern his supposed status or the position he believed himself to hold.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while Simon stood, Dositheus himself fell and died
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal standing-and-falling contrast concludes the wordplay surrounding the designation “the Standing One.”

source_issues.source_quote: ταγεὶς δὲ μετ’ οὐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας τοῖς τριάκοντα συμμαθηταῖς
source_issues.issue: The dative with the participle permits Simon to be assigned among or to the thirty fellow disciples, or possibly appointed over them. The main rendering chooses ranking among them because the preceding sentence places him second under Dositheus.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῦ μὴ αὐτὸν εἶναι νομίζειν τὸν ἑστῶτα
source_issues.issue: The main text takes μή as negating the embedded identification: Dositheus was thought not to be the Standing One. It may instead have wider scope over νομίζειν, giving “so that people would no longer think him to be the Standing One.” The alternatives differ between a negative judgment and the cessation of a positive judgment, but both are defensible from the construction.

source_issues.source_quote: Εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ ἑστώς, καὶ προσκυνῶ σε
source_issues.issue: The conjunction may introduce the consequence, “then I worship you,” or carry additive force, “I too worship you.” The main text adopts the consequential reading.

The phrase may mean that Dositheus lowered himself to the rank of the twenty-nine chiefs or that he cast himself down together with them. The main rendering chooses the rank relation because he is surrendering his leadership position.

source_issues.source_quote: εἰς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ τῆς ὑπονοίας τόπον ἔστησε τὸν Σίμωνα
source_issues.issue: The expression is unusual. The main rendering takes it as Dositheus making Simon stand in the place Dositheus had occupied in the group’s estimation. Alternatively, it may denote Dositheus’s supposed status or the position he himself believed he held. Rendering ἔστησε as “made stand” preserves the explicit standing motif without resolving the genitive phrase beyond what the context supports.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
